content: The World Health Organization (WHO) has developed comprehensive antenatal care (ANC) guidelines aimed at improving the quality of routine healthcare provided to all pregnant women and adolescent girls. These guidelines, first published in 2016, emphasize the importance of ensuring a positive pregnancy experience, which extends beyond survival to focus on maximizing health, human rights, and the potential of populations. Recognizing the critical role of ANC in promoting health and preventing disease, 14 of the 49 recommendations in the 2016 ANC guidelines address nutritional interventions during pregnancy. In April 2019, the WHO Executive Guideline Steering Group (GSG) prioritized updating two antenatal nutritional recommendations based on new evidence. These included recommendations on vitamin D supplementation and multiple micronutrient supplementation during pregnancy. The updated evidence was reviewed by an international Guideline Development Group (GDG) during an online meeting held in December 2019. The updated recommendations were developed in line with WHO’s living guidelines approach, ensuring consistency with the original 2016 ANC guideline. The updated recommendation on antenatal vitamin D supplementation applies to pregnant women and adolescent girls as part of routine ANC. WHO does not recommend routine oral vitamin D supplementation for all pregnant women to improve maternal and perinatal outcomes. Instead, pregnant women should be encouraged to maintain adequate nutrition through a healthy, balanced diet and to refer to guidelines on healthy eating. It plays a vital role in maintaining normal blood levels of calcium and phosphate, which are essential for cellular function and bone health. During pregnancy, the fetus acquires vitamin D from the mother, forming the primary source of vitamin D for infants in the first months of life, especially among breastfed infants. Vitamin D deficiency is common worldwide, with a high prevalence among pregnant women in the Middle East and Asia. Deficiency during pregnancy has been associated with conditions such as pre-eclampsia, gestational diabetes, preterm birth, and low birth weight. The updated recommendation was informed by the latest evidence, including an updated Cochrane review on vitamin D supplementation in pregnancy. The GDG considered evidence on the effects of vitamin D deficiency, as well as factors such as values, resources, equity, acceptability, and feasibility. The evidence was synthesized using the GRADE (Grading of Recommendations Assessment, Development, and Evaluation) methodology for quantitative evidence and the GRADE-CERQual (Confidence in the Evidence from Reviews of Qualitative Research) approach for qualitative evidence. The target audience for this updated recommendation includes national and local public health policymakers, maternal and child health program implementers and managers, professional bodies, healthcare professionals (such as obstetricians, midwives, nurses, and general practitioners), and academic staff involved in training the health workforce. The recommendation is relevant to all pregnant women and adolescent girls receiving ANC in healthcare facilities or community-based settings, as well as their unborn fetuses and newborns. The development of this guideline involved contributions from various WHO departments, external experts, and stakeholders. The WHO Steering Group managed the guideline development process, while the GDG, composed of international experts, appraised the evidence and formulated the final recommendation. The updated recommendation reflects WHO’s commitment to evidence-informed policies and practices, supporting the health and well-being of pregnant women and their families.
